items.name: THE ILLINOIS
items.caption: A city in the sky. A mile above Chicago. Still only on paper.
items.why_unbuilt: Wright had no secured site, client, or budget for his mile-high tower.
items.what_remains: Drawings and later visualisations preserve the ambition of a vertical city.
items.note: Announced in 1956 as a 528-storey, mile-high tower. It was a conceptual proposal, not a funded construction project. Artwork is an AI-generated interpretation; skyline and details are illustrative.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of THE ILLINOIS in monochrome engraving style.

items.name: FORD NUCLEON
items.caption: The car of tomorrow had a reactor in the back. Tomorrow never arrived.
items.why_unbuilt: The concept depended on nuclear reactors becoming small, light, and safe enough for an everyday car.
items.what_remains: A non-working 3/8-scale model and Ford brochures preserve this atomic-age vision.
items.note: The museum describes the Nucleon as more a public-relations exercise than serious development. Only a non-functional model was built; there was no running nuclear car. Artwork interprets the styling concept.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of FORD NUCLEON in monochrome engraving style.

items.name: PROJECT ORION
items.caption: A spaceship riding nuclear explosions. The future had a fallout problem.
items.why_unbuilt: Nuclear-test restrictions, fallout concerns, and withdrawn government support ended the programme.
items.what_remains: Design studies and a conventional-explosive test model survive; the nuclear spacecraft was never built.
items.note: *Period refers to the research programme. A December 1964 memo records support ending on 31 December; Smithsonian dates cancellation to 1965. Small models used conventional explosives. Artwork is a conceptual interpretation, not a specific final design.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of PROJECT ORION in monochrome engraving style.

additional_sources.name: US Department of State, 8 December 1964 memorandum
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

items.name: BOEING 2707
items.caption: America wanted its own supersonic future. The prototype never reached the runway.
items.why_unbuilt: US government funding ended in 1971 before the flight prototype was completed.
items.what_remains: The 2707-200 mockup's nose and archived drawings preserve the changing airliner design.
items.note: *1966 marks Boeing's selection for the US SST programme, not the first design work. Artwork interprets the later fixed-wing 2707-300, documented in NASA TM-109089, Figure 23; the surviving museum nose is from the earlier 2707-200 mockup. No completed flight prototype existed. Fine details and perspective are illustrative.

rating.note: Reviewed editorial score. Museum and NASA sources confirm status, chronology, surviving records and late fixed-wing configuration.

additional_sources.name: The Museum of Flight: SST cutaway drawings

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the fixed-wing Boeing 2707-300, with four underwing engines and separate tailplanes.

items.name: FUN PALACE
items.caption: A palace that could rearrange itself around its visitors. London never agreed where to put it.
items.why_unbuilt: Restrictive policies and community concerns obstructed site selection; a site was never agreed upon.
items.what_remains: Cedric Price's drawings, correspondence, planning records, and models document the adaptable structure.
items.note: Joan Littlewood and Cedric Price intended an adaptable London cultural and learning complex for actual construction. CCA dates the project 1961–1974; MoMA dates its early storyboard 1959–1961. The site was never agreed. Artwork interprets the open framework, gantry and movable spaces in the 1964 CCA brochure; it is not an exact site-specific plan. Modern Fun Palaces events are separate.

rating.note: Reviewed editorial score. Primary institutional sources confirm scope, dates and status; artwork/device review recorded separately.

additional_sources.name: MoMA storyboard collection record
additional_sources.supports: Commission, adaptable programme, intended construction and unrealised status.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of Fun Palace: open steel framework, gantry crane and movable cultural spaces.

items.name: PROJECT DAEDALUS
items.caption: A starship designed to cross the distance. Its first journey was through an engineering report.
items.why_unbuilt: Daedalus was a volunteer feasibility study, not a funded spacecraft construction programme.
items.what_remains: The 1978 report and later interstellar studies retain its two-stage fusion-probe concept.
items.note: A thirteen-member volunteer design study ran from 1973 to 1978 and published its results in 1978. It proposed an uncrewed, two-stage fusion probe for a flyby of Barnard’s Star. The study was completed, not cancelled; the proposed spacecraft was not built. Artwork interprets the staged engine bells, tanks and truss shown in BIS-hosted concept imagery. Fusion performance was theoretical, not a flight demonstration.

rating.note: Reviewed editorial score. Primary institutional sources confirm scope, dates and status; artwork/device review recorded separately.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the uncrewed two-stage Daedalus fusion probe with engine bells, fuel tanks and truss.

items.name: VENTURESTAR
items.caption: A reusable spaceship without disposable stages. Its future depended on a smaller test vehicle.
items.why_unbuilt: The VentureStar effort ended when its X-33 technology demonstrator programme was cancelled in 2001.
items.what_remains: NASA concept artwork, technical reports, and records of the related X-33 technology programme.
items.note: *1997 dates the cited NASA concept image, not the first proposal. VentureStar was the proposed full-size orbital vehicle; the partly built X-33 was a separate subscale demonstrator. NASA sources differ in shorthand February cancellation versus March funding/agreement dates: use 2001 in display copy. Never depict X-33 hardware as a built VentureStar.

sources.name: NASA programme history
sources.supports: Technology challenges; March 2001 funding decision and agreement expiry.

items.visual_brief: Broad wedge-shaped lifting body on a launch pad; distinguish full-size VentureStar from X-33 using NASA reference artwork.

rating.note: Editorial score out of 25. Institutional sources researched; qualifications and promotion blockers are recorded in note. Artwork and final review remain pending.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the unbuilt VentureStar lifting body with its broad linear aerospike base.

items.name: TATLIN'S TOWER
items.caption: A revolution imagined in iron and glass. Its headquarters remained a model.
items.why_unbuilt: Civil war, scarce material resources and the technical limits of the time kept the monument unrealised.
items.what_remains: Drawings, photographs, and reconstructed models preserve its intertwined spirals and suspended volumes.
items.note: Monument to the Third International, designed in 1919–1920. Museum Tinguely identifies civil war, resource shortages and technical limitations as contributing reasons; no single cancellation date is claimed. Centre Pompidou confirms the full monument was never built. Its displayed model is a 1979 reconstruction, not Tatlin’s original. Artwork interprets the inclined spiral framework and suspended volumes; it is not an exact engineering drawing.

rating.note: Editorial score after primary-source review. Device QA and final review are recorded in the promotion report.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of Tatlin’s unbuilt tower: inclined spiral framework and suspended geometric volumes.

additional_sources.name: Museum Tinguely retrospective
additional_sources.supports: 1919–1920 dates, unrealised status, contributing barriers and reconstructed models.

items.name: OWL 100-METRE TELESCOPE
items.caption: A mirror a hundred metres wide. The giant telescope became a study for a smaller successor.
items.why_unbuilt: A 2005 review recommended a smaller telescope because of substantial technical risks.
items.what_remains: The OWL Blue Book, concept drawings, and research that informed ESO's ELT.
items.note: ESO dates the completed concept study to 1998–2005. An international review recommended a smaller telescope due to substantial technical risks; the 100-metre OWL was not built. OWL is distinct from the later 39-metre ELT. Artwork interprets the 2004 open structure, shallow segmented optical mirror and secondary support from ESO’s archived configuration; perspective, trusswork and segment counts are illustrative. No precise site, build cost or cancellation day is asserted.
items.visual_brief: Broad segmented mirror and exposed telescope support structure, using OWL drawings rather than the ELT dome; retain scale cues.

rating.note: Editorial score after primary-source review. Device QA and final review are recorded in the promotion report.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed OWL telescope with segmented optical mirror and open steel support structure.

additional_sources.name: ESO OWL archive
additional_sources.supports: Completed study, review and recommendation for a less risky 30–60-metre telescope.

additional_sources.name: ESO FAQ
additional_sources.supports: OWL was a concept study; no current plan to build a 100-metre optical telescope.

additional_sources.name: ESO archived structural configuration
additional_sources.supports: Segmented optical mirrors and open steel alt-azimuth structure, 2004.

items.name: X-20 DYNA-SOAR
items.caption: A spaceplane before the Shuttle. Its glider stayed unfinished; its research outlived the programme.
items.why_unbuilt: The US government cancelled it in December 1963, citing no viable military mission and excessive research cost.
items.what_remains: Museum models, technical records, and photographs preserve the design and its component research.
items.note: *1959 marks Boeing's design contract on 9 November, not the earlier origins of Dyna-Soar. Boeing states cancellation on 10 December 1963, a mock-up and partly completed prototype, both later scrapped. Smithsonian preserves separate models. Air Force sources were search-visible but full-page retrieval returned 403. Do not depict a completed vehicle photograph as real: manufacturer launch/orbit artwork is conceptual.

sources.name: Smithsonian model record
sources.supports: Surviving model and December 1963 cancellation; search record accessible, page blocked.

sources.name: Air Force programme history
sources.supports: No completed glider and later use of research; search record accessible, page blocked.

items.visual_brief: Compact sharply swept delta spaceplane on a Titan booster, using a specific late configuration; show its small scale and avoid Shuttle-like engines.

rating.note: Primary/institutional review distinguishes mock-up, partial prototype and models from a completed flight vehicle.

items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed X-20 Dyna-Soar spaceplane atop its launch booster.

items.name: ROCKWELL X-30
items.caption: An airliner meant to reach orbit. Only a small tunnel demonstrator met the heat.
items.why_unbuilt: Congress ended funding in 1994 before a full-scale aircraft was built.
items.what_remains: A one-third-scale concept demonstrator and programme research preserve the idea.
items.note: NASA states that no full-scale X-30 was built. The one-third-scale concept demonstrator was tested only in a high-temperature tunnel from 1986 to 1994; it was not a completed aircraft and did not fly. Artwork reconstructs the proposed full-scale vehicle and is not documentary evidence.

rating.note: NASA directly distinguishes the tunnel demonstrator from the unbuilt full-scale aircraft; artwork and all device layouts passed review.

items.visual_brief: Sleek single-stage-to-orbit lifting-body concept, clearly labelled as reconstruction; do not depict the tunnel demonstrator as a flown vehicle.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed full-scale Rockwell X-30 aerospace plane on a runway apron.

items.name: MANNED ORBITING LABORATORY
items.caption: A secret crewed spy station. Its mockup reached orbit; the real laboratory never did.
items.why_unbuilt: Budget pressure and improving uncrewed reconnaissance led to cancellation on 10 June 1969.
items.what_remains: A flown Gemini-B capsule, mockups, prototype hardware, records, and technology reused by later programmes.
items.note: NASA distinguishes the planned 60-foot crewed stations from the 1966 test, which carried a payload-less MOL mockup and a refurbished Gemini-B capsule. Aside from long-lead imaging mirrors, NASA says no operational flight hardware existed at cancellation on 10 June 1969. Artwork reconstructs the proposal.

rating.note: NASA clearly distinguishes mockup, capsule test and prototype elements from the never-built operational station; all device layouts passed review.

items.visual_brief: Proposed cylindrical MOL station with Gemini-B capsule in orbit; label as reconstruction and do not present the 1966 mockup as the completed operational station.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed Manned Orbiting Laboratory with Gemini-B capsule in Earth orbit.

items.name: SEA DRAGON
items.caption: A rocket built like a ship and launched from the sea. Its scale stayed on paper.
items.why_unbuilt: NASA funding and institutional interest did not carry the radical low-cost concept into development.
items.what_remains: NASA-hosted feasibility reports, drawings and Robert Truax’s archived project papers preserve the design.
items.note: NASA archives Sea Dragon as a feasibility and cost study, not a flight programme. Smithsonian records the related Truax project papers and says he could not interest NASA or the USAF in later similar concepts. No full Sea Dragon vehicle or operational prototype was built; do not confuse related small sea-launch tests with this proposed super-heavy vehicle.

sources.name: NASA feasibility study, Volume 2
sources.supports: 1963 contractor feasibility/cost study and proposed launch-vehicle configuration.

sources.name: Smithsonian Robert C. Truax Collection
sources.supports: Project records and the failure to secure institutional support for related sea-launch concepts.

rating.note: NASA feasibility records and Smithsonian project papers support the distinction between the proposed full vehicle and related small sea-launch tests; reconstruction passed all device layouts.

items.visual_brief: Enormous two-stage shipyard-built rocket floating vertically at sea before launch; reconstruction only, with small support vessel for scale.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed Sea Dragon super-heavy rocket floating vertically at sea beside tiny support vessels.

items.name: PROJECT HABBAKUK
items.caption: An ice aircraft carrier meant to close the Atlantic gap. Only a lake prototype froze.
items.why_unbuilt: Resource costs, technical demands and longer-range aircraft made the full carrier unnecessary.
items.what_remains: Records, pykrete demonstrations and remnants from the small Patricia Lake prototype.
items.note: NRC Canada distinguishes the proposed massive operational pykrete airstrip from the secret experimental prototype built in Alberta. The small Patricia Lake structure tested materials and refrigeration; the full ocean-going aircraft carrier was never built.

sources.name: Operation Habbakuk: A World War II Vessel Prototype
sources.supports: Peer-reviewed account of the Patricia Lake prototype and the uncompleted full-scale proposal.

rating.note: Official and scholarly evidence clearly separates the small Patricia Lake test structure from the never-built operational carrier; reconstruction passed crop review.

items.visual_brief: Enormous flat-topped pykrete aircraft carrier in the North Atlantic; clearly label as reconstruction and distinguish it from the small Patricia Lake test structure.
items.image_alt: Artistic reconstruction of the proposed full-size Project Habbakuk pykrete aircraft carrier beside a small escort ship in Arctic waters.

items.name: PALACE OF THE SOVIETS
items.caption: A congress palace crowned by Lenin. Its foundations never became the promised skyline.
items.why_unbuilt: The German invasion halted construction; its steel was removed for wartime fortifications and bridges.
items.what_remains: Designs, models and photographs document the proposal; the site later became a pool and then the rebuilt cathedral.
items.note: *The Design Museum identifies Boris Iofan’s winning 1932 design as one of six unbuilt Moscow landmarks. Construction started in 1937 and stopped after the 1941 invasion; the steel frame was repurposed and the foundations became an outdoor pool. Models, foundations and partial lower steelwork existed, but the complete palace and Lenin-topped tower were never built. Artwork is an artistic reconstruction, not a documentary photograph.

sources.name: Imagine Moscow exhibition
sources.supports: Museum identification of the Palace within an unrealised architectural vision of Moscow.

rating.note: Museum documentation clearly distinguishes drawings, models, foundations and partial steelwork from the uncompleted full palace; original reconstruction passed responsive crop review.

items.visual_brief: Boris Iofan’s monumental stepped skyscraper proposal crowned by a vast Lenin figure; reconstruction only, distinct from the real foundations and temporary lower frame.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome reconstruction of the proposed Palace of the Soviets above its incomplete riverside foundations.

items.name: CHICAGO SPIRE
items.caption: A twisting 150-storey tower began below ground. The skyline never received its spire.
items.why_unbuilt: Financing collapsed during the global financial crisis; construction stopped and the original development ended.
items.what_remains: Project records preserve the design; its deep cofferdam was later filled for a different development.
items.source_name: Council on Vertical Urbanism / Skyscraper Center
items.note: Verified 16 October 2026 against the Council on Vertical Urbanism record and current replacement-project sources. Construction began and a deep cofferdam/foundation excavation existed, but no habitable Chicago Spire tower was completed. The current 400 Lake Shore Drive towers are a separate SOM design, not completion of the Spire.

sources.name: MAP Strategies — 400 North Lake Shore Drive
sources.supports: Replacement project account documenting the stalled Spire development, started construction and deep foundation/cofferdam left on the site.

sources.name: SOM — 400 Lake Shore Drive
sources.supports: Current replacement project is a separate two-tower design under construction, not the Chicago Spire.

rating.note: Specialist and project-team evidence separates below-ground works from a completed tower and from the replacement scheme; the original reconstruction passed responsive and device-layout review.

items.visual_brief: Santiago Calatrava’s tapering twisting residential spire above Chicago’s lakefront; reconstruction only, with a small cutaway indicating the real deep foundation works but no completed tower.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome reconstruction of the unbuilt twisting Chicago Spire above its lakefront foundation excavation.

items.name: ATLANTROPA
items.caption: Dam the Mediterranean, lower the sea, join continents. Europe’s new geography stayed on paper.
items.why_unbuilt: The scheme never gained the international authority or financing needed to reshape the Mediterranean.
items.what_remains: The Deutsches Museum preserves drawings, plans, manuscripts, photographs and publicity material from Sörgel’s project.
items.note: *1927 marks the start of Hermann Sörgel’s development of the proposal; he promoted it until his death in 1952. Deutsches Museum records document planned Mediterranean dams, major sea-level reduction and an archive of drawings, plans, manuscripts, photographs and publicity. Those records and later visualisations are evidence of design and advocacy, not a completed dam, full-scale model, operational prototype or altered sea. No Atlantropa civil works were built.

sources.name: Deutsches Museum digital catalogue
sources.supports: Archive record for photographs of Sörgel and Atlantropa drawings; surviving records are documentary material, not completed infrastructure.

sources.name: Deutsches Museum Archiv-info 2020
sources.supports: Museum account of the proposed dams, 100-metre Mediterranean lowering, 3-D visualisation and extensive archive.

rating.note: Institutional archive evidence clearly separates drawings, publications and visualisations from any constructed civil works; the original reconstruction passed responsive and device-layout review.

items.visual_brief: A map-like cutaway of the unbuilt Gibraltar dam and lowered Mediterranean shorelines; explicitly conceptual, with no implication that any full-scale works or operational prototype existed.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome reconstruction of the proposed Atlantropa dam at Gibraltar beside an imagined lowered Mediterranean basin.

items.name: TOKYO BAY PLAN 1960
items.caption: A linear megacity was to cross Tokyo Bay. The great urban spine remained a model.
items.why_unbuilt: The metropolitan reorganisation remained a conceptual master plan rather than a realised city-building programme.
items.what_remains: Plans, photographs and models preserve Tange’s proposed transport spine and modular city across the bay.
items.source_name: Harvard Frances Loeb Library — Urban Design Case Study Archive
items.note: Checked 18 October 2026. Harvard explicitly describes the proposal as never realized and preserves plan/model images. Tange Associates identifies the 1960 master plan; Mori Art Museum distinguishes conceptual city plans from realised experimental architecture. Drawings and presentation models are not completed infrastructure. Later bay bridges and reclaimed districts are separate projects. No disputed total-length claim is retained. Getty was inaccessible during this check, so Harvard replaces it as the primary status source.

sources.name: Tange Associates — A Plan for Tokyo 1960
sources.supports: Architect’s office record establishing the named 1960 proposal and its authorship.

sources.name: Mori Art Museum — Metabolism: The City of the Future
sources.supports: Museum account of the innovative marine-city project intended to span Tokyo Bay.

rating.note: Sources and scope rechecked 18 October 2026; original monochrome responsive artwork reviewed. Device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: High oblique view of Tange’s linear urban spine and branching A-frame residential modules crossing Tokyo Bay; clearly a conceptual reconstruction, not later real bridges or reclaimed districts.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome interpretation of the unbuilt Tokyo Bay transport spine, civic platforms and branching housing.

items.name: WALKING CITY
items.caption: A city that could leave town. Giant roaming pods stayed on paper.
items.why_unbuilt: A speculative architectural thought experiment, not an engineered machine or an authorised construction programme.
items.what_remains: Museum-held drawings and the Archigram archive preserve the concept; no functioning city pod was built.
items.note: Rechecked 19 October 2026. The selected version is Ron Herron’s 1964 Cities: Moving aerial perspective at MoMA, not the separate 1966 ocean drawing. MoMA describes the roaming pods as architectural commentary rather than a serious structural proposition; V&A explicitly includes Walking City among experimental projects never built. Museum drawings and later display models are not full-scale buildings, working prototypes or operational machinery. This authored architectural concept fits the collection’s design-proposal scope, but no cancellation, construction contract, technical feasibility or funding failure is invented.

sources.name: V&A — DesignLab: Exploring Skylines
sources.supports: Page 23 names Walking City among experimental projects never built.

sources.name: Centre Pompidou — Walking City
sources.supports: 1964 date, Ron Herron attribution and architectural drawing status.

sources.name: M+ — Archigram Archive
sources.supports: Preservation of the authored architectural archive.

items.visual_brief: Original interpretation of the 1964 aerial pod: elongated capsule, dark faceted upper volumes, window rows, telescopic supports and corridor. Details are not engineered plans.

rating.note: Authoritative source and scope review completed 19 October 2026; original responsive artwork reviewed. Hosted device-layout review remains a merge gate.

items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome interpretation of an unbuilt Walking City pod with faceted roof volumes and telescopic supports.

items.name: GUGGENHEIM HELSINKI
items.caption: A waterfront museum won the competition. The city voted not to build it.
items.why_unbuilt: Helsinki City Council rejected the implementation proposal on 30 November 2016.
items.what_remains: The winning competition design, renderings, model photographs and municipal decision records survive.
items.note: Rechecked 20 October 2026. Helsinki City Council minutes §306 explicitly reject implementation on 30 November 2016, 53–32. Moreau Kusunoki still identifies Art in the City as the 2015 winning competition entry. The selected period concerns that design and decision, not the earlier feasibility process. Renderings, model photographs and competition exhibitions are presentation material, not a completed museum or operational prototype. No full museum was constructed; later South Harbour projects are separate designs. The asterisk qualifies the selected proposal period, not a construction interval.

sources.name: Moreau Kusunoki — Guggenheim Helsinki
sources.supports: Winning 2015 design and its architectural configuration.

rating.note: Source, scope and responsive artwork review completed 20 October 2026. Hosted device renders and final visual review remain mandatory merge gates.

items.visual_brief: Nine low dark timber pavilions and one lighthouse-like tower at Helsinki South Harbour; clearly an unbuilt winning design, not a photograph of a completed museum.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome reconstruction of the unbuilt Guggenheim Helsinki pavilion cluster and taller glazed-crown tower.

items.name: DOME OVER MANHATTAN
items.caption: A geodesic shell would tame Midtown’s weather. Manhattan never went under glass.
items.why_unbuilt: It remained an environmental-control proposal, not a realised enclosure over Manhattan.
items.what_remains: A 1960 photographic montage, drawings and later exhibition visualisations preserve the proposal.
items.source_name: The Glass House — Never Built New York
items.note: Rechecked 21 October 2026. The Glass House and Queens Museum place Dome over Manhattan in an exhibition of projects that never came to be. The Bureau International des Expositions identifies Fuller’s 1960 proposal to cover part of Manhattan for environmental control and separately documents his built United States Pavilion at Expo 1967 Montreal. No Manhattan enclosure or functioning full-scale prototype existed; the Montreal pavilion was a separate building, not partial completion. The surviving montage, drawings, models and later visualisations are presentation material. No unsupported cancellation date, contract or funding cause is asserted.

sources.name: Bureau International des Expositions — World Expos and Architectonic Structures
sources.supports: 1960 environmental-control proposal distinguished from Fuller’s built Expo 1967 pavilion.

sources.name: Queens Museum — Never Built New York
sources.supports: Museum context and 1960 Dome over Manhattan identification.

rating.note: Museum and institutional source scope plus responsive artistic reconstruction reviewed 21 October 2026; hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Original oblique view of a transparent geodesic dome spanning a 1960 Midtown skyline; not Montreal’s Biosphere, a built enclosure or an exact engineering diagram.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome reconstruction of a vast transparent geodesic dome enclosing a mid-century Midtown Manhattan skyline.

items.name: BROADACRE CITY
items.caption: Frank Lloyd Wright spread an ideal American city across the landscape. It remained a model.
items.why_unbuilt: Broadacre City was a theoretical decentralised plan, not an implemented municipal development.
items.what_remains: A large 1934–1935 model, master-plan drawings, component studies and later revisions preserve the concept.
items.note: Rechecked 22 October 2026. MoMA identifies Broadacre City as a proposed development concept and preserves its 1934–1935 painted wood, cardboard and paper model; its current gallery label notes that Wright sought a commission but the component farm units were never built. The Frank Lloyd Wright archive separately catalogues master-plan and component studies as unbuilt projects. The approximately twelve-foot model and surviving drawings are presentation material, not a completed city or operational prototype. Later buildings and planning ideas influenced by Wright do not amount to implementation of the full master plan. The period marks continuing revisions, not construction. Artwork is an original relief-model interpretation rather than an exact copy of the museum object.

sources.name: Columbia University Avery Library — Frank Lloyd Wright drawing locations
sources.supports: Archive inventory explicitly labels the Broadacre master plan, model and components as unbuilt projects.

rating.note: Major architectural vision with a current museum record, explicit unbuilt archive classification and original responsive artwork reviewed 22 October 2026; hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Aerial relief-model interpretation of dispersed one-acre homesteads, farms, civic towers and highways; not a completed real city.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome relief-model interpretation of Broadacre City's dispersed farms, highways, civic clusters and isolated towers.

items.name: PLAN VOISIN
items.caption: Le Corbusier would replace central Paris with glass towers. The polemic stayed on paper.
items.why_unbuilt: Plan Voisin was a provocative urban proposal, not an approved or implemented redevelopment programme.
items.what_remains: Plans, axonometric drawings, a diorama and publications preserve the 1925 proposal.
items.note: Rechecked 23 October 2026. Fondation Le Corbusier identifies Plan Voisin as a 1925 Paris project and lists it among Le Corbusier’s unrealized projects. MoMA explicitly states that it was never built and describes it as a polemical proposal for transforming central Paris. Drawings, publications and the exhibition diorama are presentation material, not completed buildings, demolition works or an operational prototype. Later modernist districts influenced by similar ideas are not partial completion of this project. Artwork is an original model-like reconstruction, not an exact copy of an archival drawing.

sources.name: Museum of Modern Art — Plan Voisin for Paris
sources.supports: 1925 proposal, paper medium, polemical intent and explicit statement that the plan was never built.

rating.note: Canonical unrealised urban vision, explicit institutional unbuilt evidence and original responsive artwork reviewed 23 October 2026; hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Axonometric interpretation of cruciform glass towers, open parkland and a gridded transport system imposed beside recognisable old Paris; clearly a proposal, not a completed district.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome model-like reconstruction of Plan Voisin’s cruciform towers and geometric parkland beside old Paris and the Seine.

items.name: GREAT HALL (VOLKSHALLE)
items.caption: A colossal domed hall was drawn for the Nazi capital. It never rose beyond plans and models.
items.why_unbuilt: The regime’s Germania programme collapsed during the Second World War before the hall was constructed.
items.what_remains: Architectural drawings, photographs of planning models and a separate heavy-load test structure document the programme.
items.note: Rechecked 24 October 2026. The Danish Architecture Center identifies the Volkshalle as the intended centrepiece of Germania, describes its propagandistic purpose and explicitly states that it was never built. Surviving drawings and scale models are presentation material. Berlin’s Schwerbelastungskörper was a separate load-test structure for the proposed triumphal arch, not a prototype or foundation for the hall; built Nazi-era structures elsewhere in Berlin and later film or museum models do not constitute partial completion. The entry treats the architecture critically as totalitarian propaganda. Artwork is an original neutral planning-model interpretation without regime symbols.

sources.name: Institution of Engineering and Technology — Hitler’s Impossible City
sources.supports: Distinguishes the surviving test structure, plans and models from the unbuilt Great Hall and Germania programme.

rating.note: Explicit institutional unbuilt evidence, careful model-versus-structure qualification, critical framing and original responsive artwork reviewed 24 October 2026; hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Critical monochrome architectural-model view of the immense domed hall at the end of an empty ceremonial axis; no flags, insignia, crowds or celebratory framing.
items.image_alt: Critical monochrome architectural-model interpretation of the unbuilt Great Hall’s immense domed mass at the end of an empty axis.

items.name: SAARINEN TRIBUNE TOWER
items.caption: Saarinen’s runner-up skyscraper lost the contest, then influenced the towers that followed.
items.why_unbuilt: Eliel Saarinen’s design placed second; Howells and Hood’s winning Tribune Tower was built instead.
items.what_remains: The competition rendering, published plates and archival records preserve the influential alternative design.
items.note: Rechecked 25 October 2026. The Library of Congress identifies Eliel Saarinen’s 1922 Chicago Tribune Tower competition rendering and explicitly records its second-prize status. The Chicago Architecture Center documents the separate Howells and Hood design that won and was built. Saarinen’s rendering and later interpretive models are presentation material, not a completed Saarinen tower or construction prototype. Buildings influenced by its setbacks do not constitute partial completion of this specific entry. Artwork is an original simplified planning-model interpretation rather than a copy of the archival rendering.

sources.name: Chicago Architecture Center — Tribune Tower
sources.supports: Documents the competition and the distinct winning Howells and Hood design that was constructed.

rating.note: Clear institutional competition evidence, explicit distinction from the built winning tower and original responsive artwork reviewed 25 October 2026; hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Original simplified model interpretation of Saarinen’s broad-base, tapered vertical skyscraper; not the completed neo-Gothic Tribune Tower.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome planning-model interpretation of Saarinen’s unbuilt tapered Tribune Tower competition entry.

items.name: HYPERLOOP ONE COMMERCIAL SYSTEM
items.caption: Pods carried test passengers through a Nevada tube. No commercial route ever followed.
items.why_unbuilt: Hyperloop One shut down after failing to secure a contract for a working commercial system.
items.what_remains: Test records, photographs, prototype documentation and route studies preserve the programme.
items.source_name: Reuters — Hyperloop One to shut down
items.note: Rechecked 26 October 2026. Reuters reported Hyperloop One’s closure after it failed to win a contract for a working system, and records its 2020 passenger test. The May 2025 European Commission sector study documents the same passenger test and separates development from commercial deployment. The Nevada DevLoop, sleds and pods were real experimental hardware, not a fare-carrying intercity route or completed commercial network. Other organisations’ research does not complete this company’s programme. Artwork is an original simplified cutaway presentation model, not an exact test-pod drawing or evidence of commercial operation.

sources.name: European Commission — Hyperloop sector fact-finding study
sources.supports: Documents Hyperloop One’s 2020 passenger test as technology development rather than commercial deployment.

rating.note: Company-specific unbuilt commercial scope and prototype distinction reverified; original responsive model artwork reviewed. Hosted device-layout review remains a mandatory merge gate.

items.visual_brief: Cutaway interpretation of a passenger pod inside a long elevated low-pressure tube, with the short Nevada test installation fading into an unbuilt route; distinguish tested hardware from commercial service.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome cutaway presentation model of a test tube and pod illustrating Hyperloop One’s unbuilt commercial-system vision.

items.name: LONDON GARDEN BRIDGE
items.caption: A garden was designed to cross the Thames. The trees never reached the river.
items.why_unbuilt: The trust terminated the project after the Mayor declined guarantees for its maintenance and operation.
items.what_remains: Designs, planning records, reviews and expenditure accounts document the undelivered bridge.
items.source_name: Transport for London — Temple to South Bank footbridge

sources.name: Transport for London — Final Garden Bridge costs
sources.supports: Identifies the project as undelivered and records final expenditure rather than a completed bridge.

sources.name: Rendel — Garden Bridge independent design check
sources.supports: Describes the planted 366-metre proposed footbridge, two main river piers, trusses and copper/nickel soffit.

items.note: Rechecked 27 October 2026. TfL records 2014 planning consent, the Mayor's refusal of operating guarantees on 28 April 2017 and termination on 14 August 2017. The independent checking engineer describes the planted deck and two main river piers. Design models, planning consent, contracts and pre-construction spending do not establish a completed Thames crossing. Heatherwick's built Little Island in New York is a separate project. Artwork is an original simplified presentation-model reconstruction, not a photograph or exact engineering drawing.

rating.note: Strong garden-on-a-bridge silhouette, documented termination and public-record evidence; recognition is strongest in Britain and architecture is well represented.

items.visual_brief: Original model-like interpretation of a low planted pedestrian deck on flared piers over the Thames; clearly a proposal, not a completed London crossing.
items.image_alt: Artistic monochrome presentation model of the unbuilt London Garden Bridge, showing a planted pedestrian deck on two flared river piers.

items.name: NEWTON'S CENOTAPH
items.caption: A vast sphere imagined for Newton. The monument existed in drawings, not stone.
items.why_unbuilt: A visionary paper project, not a documented construction programme; no specific cancellation is established.
items.what_remains: Six original ink-and-wash drawings are catalogued and digitised by the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
items.note: Rechecked 30 October 2026. BnF catalogues the 1784 paper project and original drawings; the scholarly Design Arts Medias account explicitly identifies the cenotaph designs as never constructed. No funding failure, engineering impossibility, client or cancellation date is invented. This is an empty memorial concept, not Newton's tomb. Later models and this artistic reconstruction are not a completed monument.

sources.name: Library of Congress collection record
sources.supports: Imaginary memorial concept; full page inaccessible during this research.

sources.name: BnF individual drawing record
sources.supports: 1784 daytime section drawing.

sources.name: Design Arts Medias — Landscape cemetery study
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies the 1784 cenotaph designs as never built.

items.visual_brief: Spherical monument on a stepped circular base with cypress trees, derived from the original elevation; keep the complete sphere visible.

rating.note: Editorial score out of 25. Institutional sources researched; qualifications and promotion blockers are recorded in note. Artwork and final review remain pending.

items.image_alt: Original interpretive monochrome illustration of newton's cenotaph, not archival photography.

items.name: CARDIFF BAY OPERA HOUSE
items.caption: The competition was won. The opera house remained a model.
items.why_unbuilt: The project failed to secure Millennium Commission funding.
items.what_remains: Paintings, drawings and a 1995 architectural model survive in the Zaha Hadid Foundation collection.
items.note: Rechecked 31 October 2026. The Zaha Hadid Foundation explicitly states that the project lost Millennium Commission funding and was never built. Competition success, design development, paintings and the surviving 1995 presentation model are records of the proposal, not a completed opera house, construction prototype or occupied auditorium. Artwork is an original model-like interpretation, not a copy of a Foundation painting.

rating.note: A competition-winning design with a clear institutional never-built statement and exceptional silhouette; recognition is strongest among architecture audiences.

items.visual_brief: Original model-like interpretation of layered angular plates and auditorium volumes; do not copy a specific Foundation artwork or portray a completed bay building.
items.image_alt: Original monochrome architectural-model interpretation of the unbuilt Cardiff Bay Opera House competition design.

items.name: THE PEAK
items.caption: A fractured club would hover above Hong Kong. The winning design remained drawings and a model.
items.why_unbuilt: The competition-winning private club was never realised.
items.what_remains: The Zaha Hadid Foundation preserves paintings, drawings, a sketchbook and the 1983 presentation model.
items.note: Rechecked 1 November 2026. The Zaha Hadid Foundation calls The Peak the competition-winning unbuilt club of 1982–1983; MoMA independently describes the private-club design as never built. Paintings, drawings, a sketchbook and the 1983 presentation model are design records, not a completed club or full-scale structural prototype. Later built Zaha Hadid projects are separate works. Artwork is an original model-like interpretation, not a copy of a Foundation work.

sources.name: Museum of Modern Art — The Peak Project
sources.supports: Describes the competition-winning private-club design as never built and distinguishes the painting as a design tool.

rating.note: Iconic paper-architecture image and excellent museum evidence; architecture and Zaha Hadid are already well represented, reducing catalogue novelty.

items.visual_brief: Layered cantilevered plates and artificial geology above a steep Hong Kong hillside; treat paintings and the model as proposal records, not a built club.
items.image_alt: Original monochrome architectural-model interpretation of the unbuilt Peak leisure club as stacked cantilevered plates in steep terrain.
